Closing the tunnel and releasing the interface.
The packet engine is not in this build
Boreas routes packets through a shared Rust engine. This build carries the Android control surface only, so there is nothing to hand the tunnel to.
Android will not create a VPN interface without your approval. Start the tunnel again to see the request a second time.
This device cannot prepare a VPN
Another app may already hold the always-on VPN slot, or the device policy forbids VPN apps. Check Settings, then Network, then VPN.
An upstream socket could not bypass the tunnel
Boreas stops rather than send its own upstream traffic back through itself. Nothing was tunnelled.
The tunnel interface could not be created
Android refused the interface configuration. Check the addresses and routes under Settings, then Tunnel.
The new configuration needs a restart
The running session kept its previous configuration. Stop and start the tunnel to apply the change.
Every number below is generated in the app. No packets are being tunnelled and no traffic is filtered.
Runs the lifecycle and fills the counters with generated values, so the interface can be reviewed before the packet engine is linked. Debug builds only.

The engine reports counters while a session runs. Start the tunnel to collect the first set.
The engine decides what happens to every packet. These choices are handed to it when a session starts.

Android builds the tunnel interface from these values. They describe the device, not what the engine does with the packets.
The address Boreas gives the tunnel interface. Use a range that nothing else on your network uses.
Largest packet the interface will carry, in bytes. Between 1280 and 9000.
One address per line. Leave empty to keep the servers the network supplies.

Android can start this tunnel by itself and keep it running, including after a restart. Only Android can turn that on, in its own VPN settings.
Android starts this tunnel without being asked and restarts it if it stops.
Android also blocks traffic whenever the tunnel is down, so nothing leaves this device unfiltered between sessions.
This tunnel runs only while you have started it.
Boreas reads this from the running service. Start the tunnel once, or check Android\'s VPN settings.
With lockdown on, an app you exclude here gets no network at all while the tunnel is down.
By default every app uses the tunnel. Turn one off to send its traffic straight to the network.
Boreas could not read the installed app list.
Reading inside HTTPS requires a certificate that this device trusts. Boreas installs it into your personal certificate store, which you control and can remove at any time.
TLS inspection stays off until the certificate is installed.
What this certificate can and cannot do
It goes in the personal store, so only apps that opt in to personal certificates will honor it. Many apps pin their own and will not.
Removing it is an Android action, not a Boreas one. Boreas can open the screen but cannot delete it for you.
Lifecycle transitions recorded by the service, newest first. This list holds the most recent entries and is not written to disk.
Transitions appear here once you start a tunnel.

The engine speaks plain DNS today, so anything between this device and the resolver can read which names you ask for. Prefer a resolver on this network, or one you run.
One rule per line, in AdGuard or uBlock syntax. A line the engine cannot read is skipped, not fatal.
Terminate TLS for the hosts below and filter what is inside.
One name per line. Names only, never patterns or addresses.
Inspection issues a certificate for every host above, signed by a root you install on this device. Keep the list short enough to read.
Edit HTML as it arrives, inside a memory budget the engine holds.
What the router in front of this device does to a connection. The engine cannot measure it, and the answer decides whether QUIC survives.
One mapping serves every destination. The most permissive answer.
A new mapping for each destination address.
A new mapping per address and port. Choose this if you are unsure: it never claims more than is true.
